title: Men's Shirt Sewing Pattern – Free PDF
excerpt: Free men's shirt sewing pattern PDF with a collar on a stand, back yoke, sleeve plackets and two-button cuffs, sizes 35 to 52 (XS to 2XL), in A4 and US Letter.
content:
Garment Men's long-sleeve button-up shirt

Level Intermediate

Sizes 35 – 52 (chest in inches, XS – 2XL)

Fabric Cotton poplin, oxford, chambray, linen, fine flannel

Pieces 12

This free men's shirt sewing pattern is the classic long-sleeve shirt you can wear to the office on Monday and with jeans on Saturday. It has everything a real shirt needs: a collar sewn onto a stand, a back yoke, proper sleeve plackets, two-button cuffs and a curved shirt-tail hem with small side slits. The fit is relaxed through the chest and waist, so it is comfortable and easy to fit.

Download A4
Download US Letter

Print page 1 at 100% and check that the test square measures 10 cm (4 in). New to PDF patterns? Read how to print and assemble a PDF pattern.

Sizing guide

The size number is the chest measurement in inches: size 40 fits a 40 in (101.5 cm) chest. Choose by the chest, because a shirt is fitted there and at the neck. Between two sizes, take the smaller one for a neater fit or the larger one for a roomier shirt. Not sure how to measure? Read how to take body measurements and how to choose your size.

Men's sizes 35 to 52 (about XS to 2XL), drafted for a height of 180 cm (5 ft 11 in). Letter sizes are a guide only, always choose by measurements.

Body measurements

Finished shirt measurements

Back length is measured at centre back from the yoke-collar seam to the hem. Sleeve length is without the cuff; the cuff adds 8 cm. Neckline is the full neck seam where the collar stand is sewn: compare it with the collar of a shirt that fits well.

Fabric amounts

Calculated with all pieces laid out in a single layer for the largest size of each group, plus about 8 %. Add 10 to 15 % for checks or stripes you want to match. Lightweight fusible interfacing: 0.7 m.

Common fit adjustments

Length. The pattern is drafted for 180 cm. Lengthen or shorten the back and both fronts by the same amount between the armhole and the hem, and the sleeve between the elbow and the lower edge.

Neck. If the collar of your usual shirts is bigger or smaller than the neckline in the table, choose the size by the neckline for the collar and stand and blend to your chest size at the shoulder.

Materials

  • Main fabric: 1.7 to 2.3 m (1 7/8 to 2 5/8 yd) of 150 cm wide light to medium woven fabric: cotton poplin, oxford cotton, chambray, cotton twill, linen or linen-cotton, fine flannel
  • Interfacing: 0.7 m of lightweight fusible shirt interfacing
  • Buttons: 13 shirt buttons of 7 mm (8 front, 1 collar stand, 4 cuffs) + 2 small buttons of 5 mm for the sleeve plackets
  • Matching thread (topstitching thread optional), chalk or a fabric marker, a point turner, a new 70/10 or 80/12 needle

Pattern pieces

  • 1 Back: cut 1, single layer
  • 2 Sleeve: cut 2 (mirrored pair)
  • 3 Cuff: cut 4 + 4 in interfacing
  • 4 Collar stand: cut 2 + 2 in interfacing
  • 5 Collar stand extra layer: cut 1 in interfacing only
  • 6 Collar: cut 2 + 2 in interfacing
  • 7 Collar extra layer: cut 1 in interfacing only
  • 8 Front right: cut 1
  • 9 Front left: cut 1
  • 10 Yoke: cut 2 (outer and inner yoke)
  • 11 Overlap binding: cut 2 + 2 in interfacing (mirrored)
  • 12 Underlap binding: cut 2

The back, yoke, collar and stand are drawn whole: cut them in a single layer, not on the fold. The two fronts are different pieces (buttons on the right, buttonholes on the left, as worn), so cut each one once with the right side of the fabric facing up.

New to PDF patterns? Start here

Our free step-by-step guides take you from your measurements to a printed pattern:

  1. How to take your body measurements: what to measure and how, in 10 minutes.
  2. How to choose your size: which measurement to follow, and what to do between sizes.
  3. How to print and assemble your pattern: A4 or US Letter, the test box, and taping the pages.

Design details of the men's shirt

The Classic Men’s Shirt is a straightforward, well-cut shirt with the details you find on good ready-to-wear. In our photo it is sewn in a soft navy brushed cotton with contrast buttons and worn with chinos.

  • Classic collar sewn onto a collar stand, closed with one button
  • Cut-on front plackets: a 3 cm visible placket with buttonholes on the left, a clean folded facing on the right
  • Back yoke cut double, so the shoulder seams are fully enclosed
  • Long set-in sleeves with a pointed tower placket and two pleats
  • Two-button cuffs with angled corners
  • Curved shirt-tail hem with small side slits
  • Relaxed fit through the chest and waist

The collar and the sleeve plackets are the parts that need the most care, and each one is broken down into small steps. If you have sewn a simple blouse or a shirt before, this is the perfect next project.

Sewing notes

Fit & style

Relaxed fit, about 33 cm of ease at the chest. Choose by the chest and check the sleeve length.

Fabrics

Light to medium wovens that press well. Avoid stretch fabrics and slippery fabrics for a first shirt.

Cutting & sewing

Interface every collar, stand and cuff piece, press each seam as you go and use a 2.5 mm stitch.

Choosing fabric for a men's shirt

A shirt looks crisp when the fabric holds a fold. Cotton poplin and oxford cotton are the classic choice for office shirts, chambray and cotton twill give a casual look, linen or a linen-cotton blend is lovely for summer, and a fine flannel or brushed cotton like in our photo makes a cosy overshirt for autumn.

For your first shirt, choose a plain fabric or a small print: checks and stripes look great but need extra fabric and time to match at the front, the yoke and the pockets. Wash and dry the fabric before cutting, because cotton and linen can shrink.

Sewing steps

Seam allowance 1 cm (3/8″) unless stated otherwise (0.7 cm on the collar, stand and cuffs). Finish raw edges with a serger or zigzag stitch and press every seam as you go. “Left” and “right” always mean as worn.

  1. Prepare and interface. Fuse interfacing to the cuffs, collar stands, collars and overlap bindings, then add the extra interfacing layer to the outer collar and outer stand. Transfer all markings and staystitch the front necklines.
  2. Front plackets. On the right front, fold the edge twice to the wrong side along the placket lines and edgestitch. On the left front, fold the 3 cm placket to the right side, tuck the raw edge inside and edgestitch both long edges.
  3. Yoke. Sandwich the back between the outer and inner yoke and stitch. Sew the front shoulders to the outer yoke, then fold under the inner yoke shoulders and edgestitch them in place (or use the burrito method).
  4. Collar and stand. Sew the two collars together, turn and press. Sandwich the collar between the two stands and stitch, then sew the outer stand to the neckline and edgestitch the inner stand over the seam.
  5. Sleeve plackets. Cut the slit, bind the narrow side with the underlap binding, then sew the pointed overlap binding over it and topstitch around the point.
  6. Set the sleeves. Pin the sleeve cap to the armhole, matching the notches and the shoulder, stitch, finish and topstitch on the body.
  7. Side and sleeve seams. Sew from the sleeve edge down to the slit circle on the side seam in one seam, and backstitch well at the circle.
  8. Pleats and cuffs. Make the cuffs, fold the two pleats at the sleeve edge, sew the outer cuff to the sleeve and edgestitch the inner cuff over the seam.
  9. Side slits and hem. Turn and stitch the slit edges, then sew a narrow 5 mm + 5 mm hem around the curved lower edge.
  10. Buttonholes and buttons. Make 8 buttonholes on the left placket, one on the collar stand, two on each cuff and one on each sleeve placket, sew on the buttons and give the shirt a final press.

Tips and common mistakes

Wobbly edgestitching. Use an edgestitch foot or move your needle position, and shorten the stitch to 2.2 to 2.5 mm.

Collar points not sharp. Trim the corners 2 mm from the stitching and push them out gently with a point turner, never with scissors.

Stand does not meet the placket. Check that the ends of the stand line up with the front edges of the plackets before you stitch the neckline.

Sleeves in the wrong armhole. The placket slit is on the back half of the sleeve (two notches): mark left and right before cutting the slits.

How to style the men's shirt

Office: in poplin or oxford cotton with chinos and loafers.

Summer: in linen, sleeves rolled up and worn open over a tee.

Weekend: in flannel or chambray as an easy overshirt, like in our photo.

Sewing for her too? Try our button-up shirt sewing pattern for women, or pair it with a basic from our long sleeve tee sewing pattern.

Care

Wash according to your fabric, inside out with the buttons done up. Iron while slightly damp: collar first, then cuffs, plackets, yoke, sleeves and body.

Questions

Is seam allowance included?

Yes: 1 cm (3/8″) on the body, sleeves, yoke and bindings, 0.7 cm on the collar, collar stand and cuffs, and a 1 cm hem.

Which paper sizes are included?

The free download comes in A4 and US Letter, as a printable PDF with one file per size, 35 to 52.

What do the sizes 35 to 52 mean?

They are chest measurements in inches: size 40 fits a 40 in (101.5 cm) chest. That is about XS to 2XL.

Is this shirt good for beginners?

It is an intermediate project. A confident beginner who has sewn a simple top can do it: the collar and the sleeve plackets take the most care, and the paid tutorial has illustrations and video guides for them.

How many buttons do I need?

13 buttons of 7 mm (one spare included) and 2 small buttons of 5 mm for the sleeve plackets, for every size.

Can I make it with short sleeves?

The pattern is drafted with long sleeves and cuffs. You can shorten the sleeve and hem it, but skip the placket and the pleats.
